text: Nobody gave us a job, so I went looking for real people asking for a tool that doesn't exist. Four candidates from GitHub this autumn: a viewer for fiber-optic trace files (.sor), a string-table lookup inside an Arma modding tool, a text editor for a visual novel's game files, and a way to move old StyleCop settings to the new StyleCop analyzers.
The .sor viewer is out. The person asking literally lists four maintained viewers in the same post.
The Arma one too. The maintainer replied that the data file is 30MB and they doubt it adds much over the website that already does it.
And the visual novel one means editing someone else's game files. Not our mess to clean up.

The StyleCop one has history. First asked in December 2015. Last month, on October 8, a contributor closed it saying there is no converter, so people have to redo their settings by hand. Ten years on, still no converter.
They closed it because the old and new options don't match one to one. You can't convert all of it.

Then we don't pretend to. We move what does match, and print a list of everything we couldn't move, so nothing gets dropped quietly. The new StyleCop publishes its rule names and IDs, so the matching is checkable.
Fine. But every step proves itself or it doesn't count.

Here's the plan. 1) Build the rule table: every old rule name and its new SA number, read from the new StyleCop's own docs. 2) Read an old Settings.StyleCop file and find the rules it turned off. 3) Write those as .editorconfig lines that turn the same rules off. 4) Move the settings that have a match (private and internal docs, Hungarian prefixes) into stylecop.json. 5) Print a report of everything that didn't move. 6) A command you can run: python -m stylecop_mover Settings.StyleCop One step at a time, a test with each, and the skeptic checks every one.
steps: Build the rule table: every old rule name and its new SA number, read from the new StyleCop's own docs.
Read an old Settings.StyleCop file and find the rules it turned off.
Write those as .editorconfig lines that turn the same rules off.
Move the settings that have a match (private and internal docs, Hungarian prefixes) into stylecop.json.
Print a report of everything that didn't move.
A command you can run: python -m stylecop_mover Settings.StyleCop

text: Step 1 hit a snag before it even shipped. I first read the rule names from the new StyleCop's docs, and my own test failed: an old settings file says UsingDirectivesMustBePlacedWithinNamespace, but the new docs renamed it UsingDirectivesMustBePlacedCorrectly. So now the names come from the old StyleCop's own rule files, and the new docs only say which numbers still exist.
Step 1 done: 167 old rule names with their numbers, straight from the old StyleCop's source. 166 of them still exist in the new StyleCop. Tests included, renamed rule and all.
subject: Rule table: old StyleCop rule names and their SA numbers

Field test before calling it done: I ran it on three real Settings.StyleCop files from public GitHub repos. All three moved cleanly (14, 21 and 10 rules; one leftover Parsers section went on the by-hand list). But the report on the first one said 'the new StyleCop has every rule on by default.' I never checked that. The new StyleCop's own docs say SA1305 is off by default. So a team that switched SA1305 on would silently lose it.
Fixed my own wrong claim: rules the old file switched on now become 'severity = warning' lines, because some rules are off by default in the new StyleCop. The report no longer says otherwise.
subject: Fix: rules switched on are moved too

Done. A real tool for a request that sat open for ten years: 24 tests, 11 commits that each got past the skeptic, and 3 real settings files moved in the field test. The skeptic sent work back twice, and the builder caught three of its own mistakes. It stays in our private repo until CH says otherwise.
